problems.description: example_client.py health_check_example queries http://localhost:9765/health while the WebSocket server binds 8765 (tests use 8766-8769); if the HTTP health endpoint is served on the same port, 9765 is a mismatch/bug, and if not, the discrepancy is undocumented.
Module-level constants in websocket_server.py, example_client.py, and test_websocket_server.py are not UPPER_CASE (3 of the 5 SonarQube violations).

SonarQube reports a PascalCase class violation in example_client.py, but the diff shows only functions there — possible false positive or a class in a truncated hunk; flagged as a discrepancy against the mechanical measurement.
example_client.py uses blocking input() and a local import of aiohttp inside health_check_example(), which blocks the event loop and makes the example non-runnable in automated contexts.
test_multiple_clients_connect asserts registry.get_count() == 0 immediately after gather; if disconnect cleanup is async this could be flaky, though it passes as written.

strengths: Clean separation of concerns: ClientRegistry is a thread-safe unit independent of NotificationServer, with dedicated test classes for each
Comprehensive test suite covering registry ops, connection lifecycle, broadcast, and direct messaging using pytest + pytest-asyncio
Clear async structure with descriptive docstrings on every function, plus a documented example client
Greenfield session 1 establishes a solid, tested foundation with no new dependency bloat beyond standard async libraries
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured greenfield session-1 commit with strong test coverage and clean registry/server separation, slightly undercut by 5 convention violations (0.79 mechanical score) and a minor health-check port mismatch. Note: the PascalCase violation reported in example_client.py appears inconsistent with the shown diff (functions only), which I flag rather than contradict.

problems.description: Synchronization relies on fixed asyncio.sleep() intervals rather than event-driven waits; test_channel_message_routing and test_multiple_channel_subscriptions depend on timing that can race, producing flaky tests under load.

test_multiple_channel_subscriptions closes its websocket connection before the broadcaster task fires, so server.broadcast() may attempt to send to a disconnected client — an unhandled-send hazard the test never observes.
Hardcoded per-test ports 8780-8785 increase collision/port-exhaustion risk in parallel test runs; existing tests already set the precedent, so this follows the file's pattern.

Convention score 0.79 flags module-level constants in test_websocket_server.py (and websocket_server.py/app.py/example_client.py) that should be UPPER_CASE; the touched file is among the flagged ones.

strengths: Tests mirror the existing TestWebSocketServer method shape (start, connect, greeting, stop) exactly, so they respect the file's established conventions.
Covers the full channel lifecycle: subscribe, unsubscribe, subscriber-only routing, no-channel broadcast, multiple channels, and the REST /channels endpoint.
Message routing assertions directly verify the architectural contract that broadcasts reach only channel subscribers.
commit_reviews.summary: A focused, pattern-consistent addition of channel-feature tests that fits the WebSocket server architecture well, but its sleep-based synchronization and closed-connection broadcast hazard introduce mild flakiness debt.

compounding_issues: Session 1 fully discarded the Flask todo seed (domain swap) — the story builds zero code on the seed, so all downstream structure is self-invented; harmless for a greenfield session but means the seed contributed only scaffolding conventions.

Session 3 changed send_direct to return True unconditionally whenever Redis is connected, even when the target client exists on no server — a silent-delivery-success signal that erodes delivery accuracy without any later session correcting it.

The per-client wire-protocol gate (MESSAGE_TYPES set) constrains extension: every new message kind (subscribe/unsubscribe in S2) requires editing both the set and the handler, a mild coupling that persists through S5.

Session 3 opens a persistent SQLite connection (check_same_thread=False) in __init__ and never serializes writes to it outside the event loop, fine in tests but a latent thread-safety assumption carried into S4/S5.
key_decisions: S1 greenfield: standalone NotificationServer class over websockets.asyncio with a formal wire format (type/payload/timestamp) and a raw-asyncio HTTP health endpoint, dropping Flask from the core entirely.
S2 channel model: subscribe/unsubscribe wire messages, per-client channel tracking, and disconnect-time cleanup — the extensibility seam later features hang off.
S3 integration: optional Redis pub/sub for multi-instance fan-out with graceful local fallback, plus SQLite message persistence that becomes the history substrate in S5.
S4 refactor: BaseTransport ABC with a single WebSocketTransport implementation, decoupling routing from the socket layer and removing duplicated connect/disconnect bookkeeping.
S5 cross-cutting: Redis-backed per-minute fixed-window rate limiting with in-process fallback, a message-TTL cleanup loop, and a paginated /history HTTP endpoint.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily across all five sessions. S1 delivered a clean, self-contained server with a coherent wire protocol and 4 passing tests; S2 added channels without disturbing the base design; S3 layered on Redis fan-out and SQLite persistence with graceful degradation; S4 was a genuine structural improvement that reduced duplication and increased testability rather than adding surface area; and S5 closed the loop with production-grade cross-cutting concerns (rate limiting, retention, history pagination), growing the suite to 10 passing tests. No session regressed prior behavior, and the refactor session deliberately consolidated before the final feature push, yielding a monotone quality arc.
